summary: A group of mineral exploration geologists from Tucson, Arizona conditionally supports ORV regulations, but protests any implementation that fails to distinguish between recreational use and working use for mineral exploration. They argue that modern mineral exploration requires sophisticated geophysical equipment that cannot be transported by burro or backpack, making off-road vehicles essential. They support controlling recreational ORV use but insist that mineral exploration must be recognized as a vitally necessary exception on all public lands open for mineral entry, consistent with the economic and technical considerations required by the Environmental Policy Act of 1969.

statement.text:
6520 East 22nd Street Tucson, Arizona 85710
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
"C" Street between 18th & 19th Sts. N.W.
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Sir:
We, as a group of mineral exploration geologists, wish to go on record as protesting the "Review of Departmental Implementation Proposals" made by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation.
This review mentioned various uses for off road vehicles: recreation, fire fighting and tending domestic grazing animals, but there was not a single notation of their value and necessity for minerals exploration. Such a use is also important, along with fire control and care of livestock.
To quote from the Environmental Policy Act of 1969, all agencies of the Federal Government are directed to:
"identify and develop methods and procedures which will insure that presently unquantified environmental amenities and values are given appropriate consideration in decision making along with economic and technical consideration."
The required economic and technical consideration must certainly be given to mineral exploration on the public lands available for that purpose.
Spending, as we do, a great part of our working time in the mountains and deserts of the Western U. S., we realize the necessity for some type of control on the use of off road recreational vehicles in certain areas. However, a definite and clear cut distinction should be made between recreational use which can be carried out in almost any area, and the productive economic values of such vehicles. The firefighters must be allowed to go to the site of the blaze, the rancher must be able to reach his stock, and the exploration geologist must investigate mineralized zones, which are fixed, immovable, limited in individual area, and rare.

57
San Bernardino County, California, recently passed an ordinance relating to off road vehicles (County ordinance No. 1590, Sec. 2, Title 2, Division 8, Chapter 4, of San Bernardino County Code, dated 8 September, 1970). We requested an opinion on the effect of this ordinance as related to mineral prospecting and exploration from a highly regarded legal firm. To quote from the reply:
"The general mining laws provide that the public domain is open to entry for the purpose of prospecting, developing and mining, and thus those engaged in these activities may cross the surface. As a consequence, a motor vehicle engaged in prospecting, etc., may cross the surface.
"However, such permitted surface use, without the benefit of a permit from the Bureau of Land Management should not and would not include the operation of recreational vehicles such as dune buggies, motor cycles and the like."
Any restriction on ORV that does not allow for the working use of such vehicles would effectively prevent mineral exploration over large areas of the public domain, despite the fact that such areas may be legally open to mineral entry. The days when a grizzled prospector, leading a burro can discover valuable surface outcrops are long since gone. To explore for minerals today requires the use of sophisticated geophysical equipment that cannot be transported by burro or backpack. In some cases, a general area of possible geologic interest can be outlined by the use of such equipment mounted in aircraft, but more thorough investigation can only be done on the ground.
We do not question, and in fact support, regulations that will control the unrestricted use of amusement vehicles, but we strongly protest any implementation that does not allow for the economic and technical considerations required by the Act of 1969, and feel that mineral exploration should be considered as a vitally necessary exception on all public lands open for mineral entry.
Respectfully submitted,
